conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes 'No—not based on current high-quality evidence' and states that hypnosis does not show a clear, reliable advantage over other approaches, indicating that the claim is unsupported.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
**Conclusion: No—not based on current high-quality evidence.** Hypnosis/hypnotherapy may help some individuals, but research does not show a clear, reliable advantage over other cessation approaches or over minimal treatment.

The most relevant evidence is the Cochrane systematic review of hypnotherapy trials. Its comparisons include quit rates at **six months or longer**, the meaningful standard for cessation research. Cochrane’s conclusion is that there is **no clear evidence** hypnosis outperforms other approaches; if it has a benefit, available evidence suggests it is likely small. The evidence base is limited by relatively few trials, variation in hypnosis methods and comparators, and imprecision in results.  
https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD001008.pub3/information

Individual randomized trials have tested hypnosis against behavioral counseling or relaxation, but a trial alone cannot establish effectiveness—especially when the overall systematic-review evidence remains uncertain.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28891777/  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24365274/

So, hypnosis could be an optional *adjunct* if someone finds it motivating and it does not replace proven care, but it should not be presented as an evidence-based primary treatment. CDC-supported options include behavioral counseling and FDA-approved cessation medicines; using counseling and medication together gives the best chance of quitting.  
https://www.cdc.gov/tobacco/about/how-to-quit.html
